subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Cell Form Factors
description: A quick, practical guide to Cell Form Factors.

hook.text: EV battery cells come in three shapes—cylindrical cans, flat pouches, and rectangular prisms.

buildup.text: Cylindrical cells are cheap and proven—Tesla built its empire on thousands of small round cans.

discovery.text: Pouch cells are thin and flexible, letting designers fit batteries into tight or unusual spaces.

twist.text: Prismatic cells are rigid blocks that stack neatly but cost more to manufacture than cylinders.

climax.text: Tesla's new 4680 cylindrical cell is six times larger, aiming to combine cylinder cost with prismatic density.

punchline.text: The shape of the cell shapes the design of the entire car.

quiz.question: Which cell form factor did Tesla originally build its EVs around?

details.summary: EV battery cells come in three main shapes: cylindrical, prismatic, and pouch. Each form factor offers different trade-offs in energy density, cooling efficiency, manufacturability, and cost.
details.whyItMatters: The choice of cell form factor affects pack design, thermal management, crash safety, and manufacturing cost, making it a foundational engineering decision for every electric vehicle platform.
takeaways: Cylindrical cells are robust and easy to manufacture in volume
Prismatic cells pack efficiently but are costlier to produce
Pouch cells are flexible in shape but need external structural support

faq.question: Which cell form factor do most EV manufacturers prefer?
faq.answer: Tesla popularized cylindrical cells, while many Asian and European manufacturers use prismatic or pouch cells. The trend is shifting toward large-format cylindrical cells like the 4680 for cost and efficiency.

faq.question: Does the cell shape affect how quickly a battery can charge?
faq.answer: Indirectly, yes. Cylindrical cells have better surface-area-to-volume ratios for cooling, which can allow higher sustained charging rates. Pouch cells may need more elaborate cooling solutions.
